passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of three different cognitive training programs on working memory performance in adults aged 25–35. Participants were randomly assigned to one of four groups: Control (no training), Program A (visual-spatial training), Program B (verbal training), and Program C (mixed training). Each training program consisted of 30 sessions over six weeks. Working memory was assessed before and after the training period using the n-back task (2-back and 3-back). The table below summarizes the mean reaction times (in milliseconds) and standard deviations for each group after training.
stem: Which group showed the greatest improvement in working memory performance based on the reaction time data?
explanation: The greatest improvement is indicated by the lowest mean reaction time after training. Program C has the lowest mean (560 ms), indicating the fastest responses and thus the greatest improvement.
trap: Choosing Program A because it is listed first among the programs, or Control, instead of the group with the lowest post-training mean RT (Program C, 560 ms).

stem: Which experimental design element best controls for individual differences in baseline working memory capacity?
explanation: Random assignment ensures that any preexisting differences in working memory capacity are evenly distributed across the groups, thereby controlling for individual differences.
trap: Thinking a harder 3-back task controls for baseline differences; task difficulty applies to all groups and does not balance individual differences.

stem: What is the absolute difference in mean reaction time between Program A and Program C?
explanation: Program A mean = 590 ms; Program C mean = 560 ms. Absolute difference = 590 − 560 = 30 ms, option A.
trap: Subtracting in the wrong direction or using the wrong pair of programs; compare A (590 ms) with C (560 ms).

stem: Which statement is NOT supported by the data presented?

options.A: Program C produced the fastest reaction times.
options.B: All training programs improved reaction times relative to Control.
options.C: Program B had the smallest standard deviation.
options.D: Program A had a higher mean reaction time than Program B.

explanation: Standard deviations: Control 45, Program A 50, Program B 48, Program C 47. Program B’s SD (48) is not the smallest (Control’s 45 ms is), so statement C is not supported.
trap: Assuming the lowest-mean group also has the lowest SD; Control has the smallest SD (45 ms).

stem: By what percent was the mean reaction time of Program C lower than that of the Control group?
explanation: Correct: A) (650 - 560)/650 x 100 = 13.8%. Why the others are wrong: B) 16.1% divides the 90 ms drop by the Program C mean (560) instead of the Control mean. C) 9.2% is the 60 ms Control-minus-Program A difference expressed against the Control mean (60/650). D) 86.2% is Program C's mean as a percent of Control (560/650), not the reduction.
trap: Dividing the difference by the Program C mean (90/560 = 16.1%) or reporting the remaining percent (86.2%) instead of the reduction relative to Control.
